newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: APEC heads towards landmark deal on high-tech trade.
newsitem.headline: APEC heads towards landmark deal on high-tech trade.

text.p: APEC officials on Thursday hammered out details of a U.S.-inspired plan to free global trade in computers and parts worth $1.8 trillion.

But while the officials worked smoothly indoors, protesters took to the streets of Manila in unprecedented opposition to their plans to create the world's largest free trade zone embracing half of humanity around the Pacific Rim.
Leaders of the 18-member Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum are expected to endorse the plan to axe tariffs on information technology at a summit on Monday.
"This could be a real landmark for APEC," said U.S. Undersecretary of State Joan Spero.
More than 1,000 demonstrators tried to march on the Philippine presidential mansion but were blocked by riot police.
Roman Catholic priests were prominent among the generally good-humoured crowd, some wearing masks of U.S. President Bill Clinton and Philippine head of state Fidel Ramos.

After a two-hour standoff, during which the demonstrators created traffic gridlock by singing and dancing in the streets, groups of protesters scattered into side streets where they were chased by baton-wielding police.
Critics ranging from Mexican peasant leaders to Canadian trade unionists say APEC's plans would throw small businessmen and craftsmen out of work.
They fear that big corporations with no national loyalties will destroy the environment and turn poor Asia-Pacific nations into manufacturing sweatshops.
"Human Rights, Worker Rights" chanted sari-clad Indian women protesters marching through Manila's Makati financial district as part of the most vocal opposition ever at an APEC forum.
"Our call here is 'junk APEC'," said Satur Ocampo, spokesman for the People's Conference Against Imperialist Globalisation.
The protests highlighted the challenges of creating a borderless economy among countries riven by economic disparities and political differences.
APEC includes the United States and Japan as well as nations such as China struggling against poverty.

Leftist groups are planning marches, motorcades and even a protest flotilla of fishing boats involving tens of thousands of people as APEC leaders prepare for their fourth annual summit in Subic Bay north of Manila.
Foreign and economic ministers arrived in Manila on Thursday for pre-summit discussions.
Ramos toured the summit site, inspecting luxury villas where world leaders will freshen-up for their meeting, and even testing out a brand new golf course.
"Sustainable development is the bottom line in APEC, not profit," he said.

Until 1992, Subic Bay was a vital U.S. naval base. Now it is a symbol of the Philippines' economic renaissance, an industrial estate with an attached country club on jungle-clad slopes four hours drive from Manila past an active volcano.
Among leaders expected are Clinton, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and Chinese President Jiang Zemin.
The United States is pressing for the elimination of all tariffs on information technology by 2000, but it was not clear whether the APEC summit would endorse this or propose a more modest target.
Washington wants APEC's backing before putting the plan before the first ministerial meeting of the World Trade Organisation in Singapore next month.
"The Is haven't been dotted and the Ts haven't been crossed," said Spero, who added that trade in information equipment was worth an annual $1.8 trillion.
The United States currently accounts for 60 percent of world trade in information technology products.
Security was tight as some 6,000 delegates and journalists streamed into Manila. Two bomb scares on Wednesday night turned out to be security drills.

Delegates were whisked into Manila down special "friendship lanes" past queues of cars. A street vendor was killed by a speeding television van in one of the lanes on Thursday, and in a separate accident three pedestrians, including a woman and her five-year-old son, were injured.
